title: Async batcher -> handoff profiling journal
content:
Purpose:
This is a working journal capturing an end-to-end profiling sweep focused specifically on the async batcher -> handoff boundary. Goal: identify why a small slice of traces (p99) show multi-second spikes even when model-forward and token emit look fine in aggregate.

Quick summary:
- E2E observed (sample window 2025-11-02 -> 2025-11-08, mixed dev traffic): p50=180ms, p95=340ms, p99=1,270ms.
- Handoff stage (async-batcher.handoff) dominates p99: p50=12ms, p95=28ms, p99=720ms for handoff alone.
- Key correlated signals: thread contention on handoff mutex, high wait-time for batch assembly when concurrent warmup KV misses exist, intermittent serialization stalls during buffer-copy for large batched payloads.

Data collection & method:
- Trace selection: random sample of 20k requests, stratified by seq_len buckets: {short: 1-64, mid: 65-256, long: 257-1024}. We oversampled `mid` bucket because most production traffic sits there.
- Instrumentation points: request-received, tokenizer, preprocessor, async-batcher.enqueue, async-batcher.handoff, batch-build, model-forward, kv-cache.lookup, kv-cache.update, kv-prefetch, emit-serialize, egress.
- Additional metrics correlated: cpu-steal, thread-pool-runq, mutex-wait-count (per-thread), memcpy-bytes, nvlink-util (for dedicated hosts), GC-pause (JVM worker only).
- Replay microbench: 2k synthetic traces replayed into a staging cluster with sampling hooks that attach unique IDs; enabled debug tracing on async-batcher and kv-cache for 1 hour.

Representative latency breakdown (median / p95 / p99) for the `mid` seq_len bucket (values in ms):
- tokenizer: 2 / 4 / 6
- preprocessor: 4 / 9 / 14
- async-batcher.enqueue: 3 / 8 / 20
- async-batcher.handoff: 12 / 28 / 720  <-- huge tail here
- batch-build: 8 / 18 / 60
- kv-cache.lookup (per request): 6 / 15 / 160 (cold miss spikes visible)
- model-forward: 110 / 230 / 340
- emit-serialize: 16 / 30 / 46
- egress network: 7 / 12 / 18
- e2e totals (observed): 180 / 340 / 1270

What we saw in traces:
- Two dominant p99 phenotypes emerged in the handoff stage:
  1) "Lock convoy" traces: multiple worker threads attempting to hand off partial batches simultaneously run into a mutex/queue head lock in async-batcher.handoff. When queue head is contended, a single slow worker holds the lock while performing a buffer copy (memcpy) of ~1-3MB - this amplifies latency for all awaiting requests.
  2) "KV warmup cascade": a request missing in KV cache triggers a synchronous prefetch path during handoff in current staging config (we temporarily enabled `kv-prefetch-on-handoff=true`). The prefetch blocks the handoff lock until the KV backend responds or times out; if the backend experiences transient slowness (observed 50-150ms spikes on a few calls), the handoff p99 climbs sharply.

Traces examples (notes from two real p99 traces):
- Trace A (mid bucket): request queued at 12:13:02.120 -> handoff entered at 12:13:02.145 -> lock acquired -> starts memcpy -> memcpy stalls (memcpy time 520ms) -> lock released -> batch build resumes -> model-forward -> total e2e 1280ms.
- Trace B (mid bucket): queue->handoff->kv-cache lookup miss -> synchronous prefetch invoked while holding handoff lock -> kv backend 190ms response -> update kv-cache -> lock released -> subsequent batch build -> e2e 1420ms.

Root cause hypotheses and evidence: 
- Hypothesis 1: handoff uses coarse-grained locking around both queue pointer and buffer-copy. Evidence: flamegraphs from staging show a large flat region in async-batcher.handoff with memcpy dominating CPU wake times. Also mutex-wait histograms show long tail.
- Hypothesis 2: prefetching while holding handoff lock (optimistic correctness but bad for latency) is causing cascades when KV backend is flaky. Evidence: traces with kv-prefetch-on-handoff=true have higher p99 in handoff compared with control. Replays disabling this flag removed many of the kv-prefetch tail traces.
- Hypothesis 3: large batched payloads (when many short requests batch together) increase memcpy time and scale superlinearly under memory bandwidth pressure on hosts. Evidence: correlation between memcpy-bytes and p99 across traces; hosts with heavy local NVMe egress also showed worse memcpy times.

Microbench experiments run:
- Exclusive memcpy microbenchmark: measured memcpy throughput across csr/host machines; observed stalls when concurrent network egress > 500MB/s.
- Handoff lock striping: tested prototype with per-shard handoff queues (8 shards). Result: p99 for handoff reduced from ~720ms -> ~110ms in synthetic replay, p95 unchanged.
- Prefetch change: toggled kv-prefetch-on-handoff=false and enabled a background async prefetch pipeline that does not hold handoff lock. Result: p99 handoff slices with kv-miss reduced by ~85%.

Operational notes:
- The issue reproduces on both Hosted and Dedicated clusters, though on Dedicated the p99 amplitude is lower when async-batcher thread-pool sizes are tuned per-CPU.
- Stack: Go runtime (async-batcher service) + C memcpy path via cgo for batch buffer consolidation. GC was minimal in these traces.

Immediate mitigations (short-term):
- Flip kv-prefetch-on-handoff -> false in staging and canary for 24h (JIRA-RT-6321).
- Backport handoff lock striping prototype as feature-flagged change for canary(8-shard) to reduce convoy risk.
- Add memcpy-bytes and memcpy-duration metrics to the async-batcher span emitted to tracing to make the root cause visible in prod dashboards.

Longer-term recommendations (product + infra):
- Re-design handoff so that any external IO (KV prefetch) is always async and never held while holding the handoff lock.
- Implement per-client/route batch sharding heuristics so very large batch buffers aren't formed from many short requests. Consider max-aggregate-bytes cap per batch.
- Introduce backpressure signals from the memcpy path (or chunked copy) to avoid long contiguous memcpy under memory pressure.
- Run memory bandwidth benchmarking as part of dedicated host pre-flight to identify hosts likely to show high memcpy durations under load.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- What is the expected consistency model for kv-prefetch currently? If async prefetch yields correctness issues with certain routes, need to catalog those routes and add an allowlist.
- Are there other places where we synchronously call network IO while holding critical locks? Should do a lint scan.
- Does cgo memcpy path add unexpected safepoints in the Go scheduler that amplify tail latency? Need a deeper runtime analysis (Tomás to take).

Next actions (owner assigned):
- Elena: roll kv-prefetch-on-handoff=false to canary by 2025-11-13 and monitor p99 for 48h.
- Marcus: land lock striping feature-flag prototype PR for canary by 2025-11-18.
- Sana: add memcpy-duration and memcpy-bytes to tracing and dashboard panels (Grafana) by 2025-11-17.

Notes to self (brain dump):
- Avoid moving heavy copy logic into hot lock region. Even if it simplifies invariants, the tail amplification cost is huge.
- Remember to annotate traces with host-level mem bw counters next run.
- Add a tiny synthetic test that forces many short requests to coalesce into a single batch; can reproduce the memcpy convoy fast.

Appendix: small timeline of experiment runs (timestamps UTC):
- 2025-11-02 03:00: enable debug tracing on staging (2 hours)
- 2025-11-03 11:00: run replay 2k traces (baseline)
- 2025-11-04 09:30: toggle kv-prefetch-on-handoff=true for experiment (observed p99 up)
- 2025-11-06 15:00: run lock striping prototype replay (8 shards)
- 2025-11-10 08:00: disable kv-prefetch-on-handoff in staging; monitor

End of journal entry.
